newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: FOCUS - Taiwan set to import diesel, raise exports.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Taiwan set to import diesel, raise exports.

text.p: A looming switch to cleaner diesel is causing problems for Taiwan's state-owned Chinese Petroleum Corp (CPC), industry sources said on Monday.

They said CPC needed more time than the government wanted to give it to gear up to produce 0.05-percent sulphur diesel instead of the 0.3 percent sulphur fuel in use now, which could mean it would have to import diesel for the first time in several years.

CPC is also under time pressure from competitor Formosa Petrochemical Corp, a unit of the Formosa Plastics Group, due to open a new 300,000-barrel-per-day (bpd) refinery by early 1999, the sources said.
Formosa would have another 150,000-bpd of capacity ready by 2000 to lead the race for domination of the diesel market, now a CPC monopoly, they said.

The government, worried by pollution, wants the cleaner diesel in use by the middle of next year. CPC has recommended July 1999 as the target date, starting in the cities of Taipei, Kaohsiung and Taichung.
"We have to be sure that before the target date, we are fully ready," a CPC source said. "There are still a lot of points we have to make sure of before taking on this kind of commitment."
The company needs time to build desulphurising units to produce the cleaner diesel. "We would be able to produce 0.05 percent diesel by July 1999," the source said.
A Formosa source said its new refinery will have two desulphurising units, each capable of producing 120,000 bpd of 0.05-percent sulphur diesel when the first phase is opened in 1999.
When completed, that figure will rise to 130,000 bpd, he said, predicting Formosa could become Taiwan's number one supplier of diesel with 45.4 percent of the market by 2000.
The CPC source acknowledged Formosa could grab the lead if the use of the cleaner diesel is enforced before mid-1999.
CPC might be forced to import lower sulphur diesel until it could produce its own if the government decided to enforce the new regulation next year, the source said.
Taiwan now consumes 2.5 million to 3.2 million barrels of 0.3-percent sulphur diesel a month, all produced domestically.

Trade sources said CPC would incur high costs if it imported the more expensive low sulphur diesel which costs around 90 cents per barrel more than the normal grade, now around $27 a barrel, on a free-on-board basis.
That premium could rise with CPC buying in competition with South Korea and Japan for the 0.05-percent grade, mainly imported from the U.S Gulf Coast and Algeria.

Trade sources said one alternative was for CPC to refine more light crude oil, which contains very low amounts of sulphur, to meet the required quality. Such crude, however, is more expensive than the grades CPC usually refines for diesel.
To offset higher costs, whichever option it chooses, CPC would need to boost its exports of 0.3 percent sulphur diesel to a region where South Korea is fast emerging as a major exporter.

A rise in capacity at CPC's Kaohsiung and Taoyuan refineries in late 1995 to 770,000 bpd from 570,000 bpd allowed the company to raise exports. It now ships an average of three 250,000-barrel cargoes per month by spot and term sales.
With the entry of Formosa and a Tuntex Group refinery scheduled for the turn of the century, Taiwan might become another major diesel exporter in Asia, traders said.
Formosa aims to export 80,000 bpd of diesel to the region, especially to China.
-- Singapore Newsroom (+65-870 3084)
